passage:
At fifteen, Ujjwal noticed that the words on a printed exam paper swam, while the same questions read aloud made perfect sense. The humming lights in the hall gave him a headache by the second page. He told Sabina, the school counsellor, 'I know the material. I just can't get it out of print fast enough.' She listened, and together they wrote a note for the teachers asking for extra time and a quiet room. Ujjwal's next test score matched what he said in class.

At twenty-five, Ujjwal worked as a designer at a small studio. He kept his desk by the window, wore noise-cancelling headphones for the first two hours, and set his messages to arrive in batches at eleven and four. Big tasks were split into a list on the wall. When his colleague Yogesh asked why he never answered chats instantly, Ujjwal said, 'I do my best thinking in long blocks, and I check in on schedule. If something is urgent, come to my desk.' Yogesh shrugged, then said he would try the same for his own afternoons.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal and Sabina ask the teachers for?
qa.a: Extra time and a quiet room.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal's handling of his own needs change between fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: At fifteen he saw what got in his way and asked the counsellor to help him request extra time and a quiet room. At twenty-five he had built his own working systems, from a window desk and headphones to batched messages and a task list.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal likely feeling when he told Sabina he knew the material?
qa.a: Frustration that his knowledge was not showing on paper, along with some hope that someone would listen.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do to support a colleague who works in a different pattern?
qa.a: Respect the schedule, go to the desk for urgent things, and ask what setup helps instead of assuming slowness.

grounding: One person recognises and asks for support for attention and sensory needs at fifteen, then builds lasting work systems at twenty-five.
